docs.title: GravLang
docs.text: GravLang is a dynamically typed, interpreted programming language with a clean syntax that bridges imperative control flow with functional features (lambdas) and object-oriented paradigms.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Dynamic Typing: No need to declare variable types.
  • First-Class Functions: Anonymous functions (lambdas) can be passed around and returned.
  • Robust Error Handling: Full try / catch / finally support.
  • Advanced Control Flow: else and finally blocks for while and for loops.
  • Object-Oriented Programming: Classes, methods, and single inheritance.
  • Modular: Import other .grav files easily.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Save this file as hello.grav:

# This is a comment
let message = "Hello, World!";
print(message);

func fib(n) {
    if (n <= 1) { return n; }
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}

print("Fibonacci of 10 is:");
print(fib(10));

Run it via the terminal: 

python main.py hello.grav

Or open the interactive GUI debugger: 

python main.py

docs.title: Built-in Functions
docs.text: GravLang comes with a standard library of built-in functions available in the global scope.

docs.title: I/O
docs.text:
• print(*args) Outputs arguments to the console.

  • input(prompt="") Prompts the user for input and reads a line from stdin as a string.

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
• len(value) Returns the length of a string, array, or dict. Raises an error for other types.

  • type(value) Returns a string representing the type of the value (e.g., "null", "bool", "int", "float", "string", "array", "dict", or the class name of an object).

  • hasAttr(obj, name) Returns true if the given instance object has an attribute matching the name string.

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
• toInt(value) Converts the value to an integer. Raises an error if conversion fails.

  • toFloat(value) Converts the value to a float. Raises an error if conversion fails.

  • toString(value) Converts the value to its string representation (including robust serialization for arrays and dicts).

docs.title: Array Operations
docs.text:
• push(arr, value) Appends value to the end of arr. Returns the mutated array.

  • pop(arr) Removes and returns the last element of the array.

  • remove(arr, index) Removes and returns the element at the specified index.

  • contains(arr, value) Returns true if value exists inside arr.

  • reverse(arr) Reverses arr in place and returns it.

  • sort(arr) Sorts arr in place. Elements must be comparable.

docs.title: Dictionary Operations
docs.text:
• keys(dict) Returns an array of all keys in dict.

  • values(dict) Returns an array of all values in dict.

  • has(dict, key) Returns true if key exists in dict.

  • del(dict, key) Deletes the key from dict. Raises an error if the key does not exist.

docs.title: Classes & Object-Oriented Programming
docs.text: GravLang supports object-oriented programming via classes and single inheritance.

docs.title: Defining a Class
docs.text:
Classes are defined using the class keyword.

To initialize instances, you can define an init method. Instance methods are defined inside the class block using func.

class Animal {
    func init(name) {
        self.name = name;
    }

    func speak() {
        print(f"{self.name} makes a noise.");
    }
}

docs.title: Instantiation
docs.text:
To instantiate a class, call it like a function:

let pet = Animal("Dog");
pet.speak(); # Dog makes a noise.

docs.title: The self Keyword
docs.text:
The self keyword refers to the current instance of the class. It is required to access or modify instance properties from within a class method.

class Counter {
    func init() {
        self.count = 0;
    }

    func increment() {
        self.count += 1;
        return self.count;
    }
}

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
GravLang supports single inheritance using the extends keyword. A subclass inherits all methods from its parent class.

class Dog extends Animal {
    func speak() {
        print(f"{self.name} barks!");
    }
}

let fido = Dog("Fido");
fido.speak(); # Fido barks!

Note: If you override init, the parent class's init is not implicitly called. You can, however, manually invoke methods if required.

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
You can check an object's type and its properties using built-in functions:

let obj = Animal("Cat");

print(type(obj)); # "Animal"
print(hasAttr(obj, "name")); # true

docs.title: If / Elif / Else Statements
docs.text:
GravLang uses standard if, elif, and else constructs. Parentheses around conditions are optional but idiomatic.

let score = 85;

if (score >= 90) {
    print("Grade: A");
} elif (score >= 80) {
    print("Grade: B");
} else {
    print("Grade: C");
}

Note: The logical operators are and, or, and not.

if (score > 50 and not is_absent) { ... }

docs.title: Loops
docs.text: GravLang provides robust loop constructs, including advanced else and finally blocks for loops.

docs.title: While Loop
docs.text:
Standard while loop with optional else and finally blocks.

let i = 0;
while (i < 5) {
    print(i);
    i += 1;
}

docs.title: For Loop
docs.text:
Standard C-style for loop with init; condition; update:

for (let i = 0; i < 5; i += 1) {
    print(i);
}

docs.title: For-In Loop
docs.text:
Iterate over an array (iterable):

let arr = [10, 20, 30];
for (item in arr) {
    print(item);
}

docs.title: Loop else and finally
docs.text:
GravLang loops can optionally include else and finally blocks: - else: Runs ONLY if the loop finishes naturally (i.e., condition becomes false or iteration ends) and was NOT terminated by a break. - finally: Runs unconditionally after the loop, regardless of how it ended.

for (item in [1, 2, 3]) {
    if (item == 5) {
        print("Found 5!");
        break;
    }
} else {
    print("5 was never found.");
} finally {
    print("Loop execution completed.");
}

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
GravLang supports robust error handling using try, catch, and finally, as well as raising errors using throw.

try {
    let result = 10 / 0;
} catch (err) {
    print("Caught an error:");
    print(err);
} finally {
    print("Always runs.");
}

docs.title: Throwing Errors
docs.text:
You can raise exceptions using the throw keyword:

if (score < 0) {
    throw "Score cannot be negative!";
}

docs.title: Data Structures
docs.text: GravLang provides robust composite data structures natively: Arrays and Dictionaries.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
Arrays are ordered sequences of values. They are mutable, 0-indexed, and can contain mixed types.

let arr = [1, "two", 3.0, [4]];

docs.title: Access and Assignment
docs.text:
let first = arr[0];
arr[1] = 2;

docs.title: Slicing
docs.text:
GravLang supports array slicing arr[start:stop]:

let nums = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50];
let slice1 = nums[1:3]; # [20, 30]
let slice2 = nums[:2];  # [10, 20]
let slice3 = nums[3:];  # [40, 50]

docs.title: Array Built-ins
docs.text:
GravLang provides multiple built-in functions for array manipulation:

  • push(arr, value): Appends value to the end and returns the mutated array.
  • pop(arr): Removes and returns the last element.
  • remove(arr, index): Removes and returns the element at the specified index.
  • contains(arr, value): Returns true if the array contains the value.
  • reverse(arr): Reverses the array in place.
  • sort(arr): Sorts the array in place (elements must be comparable).
let letters = ["a", "b", "c"];
push(letters, "d");
pop(letters);

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text:
Dictionaries (dicts) store key-value pairs. Keys can be strings, integers, or floats.

let dict = {
    "name": "GravLang",
    "version": 1.0,
    1: "one"
};

docs.title: Access and Assignment
docs.text:
print(dict["name"]); # GravLang
dict["author"] = "Open Source";

docs.title: Dict Built-ins
docs.text:
GravLang provides built-in functions for dictionaries:

  • keys(dict): Returns an array of all keys.
  • values(dict): Returns an array of all values.
  • has(dict, key): Returns true if the key exists in the dictionary.
  • del(dict, key): Deletes the key from the dictionary. Raises an error if the key is missing.
let k = keys(dict);
if (has(dict, "version")) {
    del(dict, "version");
}

docs.title: Length
docs.text:
You can get the number of items in both arrays and dictionaries using len():

len([1, 2, 3]);       # 3
len({ "a": 1 });      # 1
len("hello world");   # 11

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Functions in GravLang are first-class citizens. They can be stored in variables, passed to other functions, and returned from functions.

docs.title: Function Declarations
docs.text:
Functions are defined using the func keyword. Parentheses are required. 

func add(a, b) {
    return a + b;
}

print(add(2, 3)); # Output: 5

If a function does not explicitly use return, it implicitly returns null.

docs.title: Anonymous Functions (Lambdas)
docs.text:
You can define inline anonymous functions, which evaluate to function objects.

let multiply = func(a, b) {
    return a * b;
};

print(multiply(4, 5)); # Output: 20

Because functions are first-class citizens, you can pass them as arguments (higher-order functions):

func operate(a, b, op) {
    return op(a, b);
}

let result = operate(10, 5, func(x, y) {
    return x - y;
});
print(result); # Output: 5

docs.title: Variadic Arguments (Spread Operator)
docs.text:
GravLang supports variadic arguments via the ...rest spread operator in the parameter list. It bundles all remaining arguments into an array.

func printAll(first, ...rest) {
    print("First argument:", first);
    print("Remaining arguments:", rest);
}

printAll(1, 2, 3, 4);
# First argument: 1
# Remaining arguments: [2, 3, 4]

docs.title: Scope and Closures
docs.text:
Functions in GravLang create a new local environment. They can capture variables from their surrounding scope (closures).

func makeCounter() {
    let count = 0;
    return func() {
        count += 1;
        return count;
    };
}

let counter = makeCounter();
print(counter()); # 1
print(counter()); # 2

docs.title: Variables & Data Types
docs.text: GravLang is a dynamically typed language, which means you do not declare types for variables. Type checking happens at runtime.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Variables are declared using the let keyword. Once declared, you can assign them new values without let.

let x = 10;
x = "Now I am a string!";

let y = 3.14;

Variables can also be modified using augmented assignment operators: +=, -=, *=, /=, //=, %=.

let count = 0;
count += 1;
count *= 10;

docs.title: Data Types
docs.text: GravLang supports several primitive and composite data types natively.

docs.title: 1. Integers
docs.text:
Whole numbers.

let age = 30;

docs.title: 2. Floats
docs.text:
Decimal numbers.

let pi = 3.14159;

docs.title: 3. Strings
docs.text:
Strings can be defined using double quotes "". GravLang also supports f-strings for string interpolation using f"...".

let name = "Alice";
let greeting = f"Hello, {name}!";

docs.title: 4. Booleans
docs.text:
true or false (case-sensitive).

let is_valid = true;
let is_finished = false;

docs.title: 5. Null
docs.text:
Represents the intentional absence of any value. The keyword is null (not None or nil).

let empty = null;

docs.title: 6. Arrays (Lists)
docs.text:
Ordered sequences of items, separated by commas, enclosed in square brackets []. Arrays are mutable.

let nums = [1, 2, 3];

docs.title: 7. Dictionaries (Dicts)
docs.text:
Key-value pairs enclosed in curly braces {}. Keys can be strings, integers, or floats. Values can be of any type.

let person = { "name": "Bob", "age": 25 };

docs.title: Type Conversion
docs.text:
GravLang provides built-in functions to safely convert between data types: - toInt(value) - toFloat(value) - toString(value)

let n = toInt("42");
let text = toString(100);
